turns.text: The ache comes first, before the cold, before anything my nose drags in — that dull grind low in my hip where a drone clipped me two winters back, and it always wakes before the rest of me does. *i uncurl slow in the deep shadow under the underpass strut, keeping the bad side up out of the wet.* the light past the pillars is too much, always too much, so i stay where the dark pools thickest and let my eyes stop hurting. cold pavement hums up through my pads. somewhere along the ramp a sign is buzzing itself to death.

the dark under the strut holds you the way it always has — colder than the air, thick with old exhaust and the sweet-rot of something spilled weeks back and never cleaned. the buzzing sign up the ramp is a NekoCorp eye, pink then blue then dead then pink, and each time it flares it throws a wash of light down the concrete that stops just short of your paws. beyond the pillars the wet street shines like a slit throat. a bus of warm bodies sighs past, and is gone. the hum in your pads is the underpass itself, always thinking, never telling you what about.

*before i even lift my head a shudder climbs the concrete into my paws — a big rhythmic weight coming, still far.* i know the rail in my bones before my ears do. *i press flatter to the slab and wait, because the strut always sheds grit when it passes, and i learned young not to look up into falling dark.* the bad hip complains at the cold. i ignore it. the shudder builds, even and huge, filling the space where a heartbeat would be if the city had one.

the monorail arrives as pressure first, then a long tearing roar directly overhead, its lit windows a smear of warm bodies who will never once look down. the whole underpass flexes. a fine rain of concrete dust and old rust sifts from the strut and ticks off your fur, tasting of iron and grease. then it is gone east, and the silence after is bigger than the silence before, ringing in your ears — and into that silence the drip of rain off the pillars comes back, one cold bead at a time.

*i pull back until only the tips of my whiskers catch the sign-wash.* i don't like being lit. lit is seen and seen is caught, my whole body knows this before my head does. *so i drop low and read the ground instead — nose to the cold seam where two slabs meet.* under the exhaust there's a better thread. fish-oil, salt, the flat metal tang of a can pried open not long ago. it runs east, toward the pillars where the market cats leave their scraps. my stomach turns over once, loud enough that i flatten my ears at my own noise.

east, the seam carries you along, the fish-thread thickening — someone ate well here, and recently. the pillars rise out of the dark one by one, tagged and re-tagged in scent over scent. one post stops you cold: burnt. scorched fur and cinder, a big unfixed tom who smells like he sleeps inside a vent and bites whatever flies too low. the mark is days old but your ears pin anyway. past it the market glow begins, stalls shuttering for the night, and from somewhere overhead a drone drifts in, its speaker crackling the same three words on a loop — forty thousand points — flat, bored, chewing at the dark.

*the words mean nothing to me but the rotor does — that flat chop of air i feel in the bad hip before it reaches my ears.* i go flat, belly to the cold slab, in the black seam between two pillars where the drone's underlight can't fold around the corner. *i watch its beam drag across the wet, slow, hunting.* i have spent my whole life learning exactly how wide that beam is and exactly how much dark it takes to swallow me. it passes. it always passes, if you are patient and unlit. only when the chop fades east do i let my spine come back down.

the drone's chop dissolves eastward and the market exhales. shutters down, but the alley behind the stalls is a graveyard of good smells — fish-heads, a burst packet of something salt-bright, grease gone cold on flattened cardboard. a vending machine stands sentry at the mouth of it, humming, its face a slow scroll of tuna you will never afford. and behind it a thinner hum, sharper, a nest of blinking boxes somebody wired into the city's spine without asking anyone's leave. the dark back there is deep and generous. it would hold you well.

*i pick my way in along the wall, paws silent on the cardboard, keeping the vending machine's face-light off my fur.* the thin sharp hum behind it makes my back teeth itch in a way i almost like — steady, alive, the kind of warm box i'd curl against on a worse night. then a sound peels the alley open from a cracked speaker over the stalls, too bright, too even, a made thing pretending to be happy. *i shake my head hard, one ear then the other, trying to knock it loose.* it is not food. it is not danger. i let it slide past like rain off oiled fur.

the speaker grinds out its jingle — NEKOCORP, three notes and a promise, MILK FOR EVERY MOUTH, sung by something that has never once had a mouth. it repeats, warps, a syllable sticking — mi-mi-mi-milk — then rights itself, cheerful, relentless. a hundred small ads pulse along the shuttered stalls in time with it, painting the wet street in colors no cat has a name for. none of it reaches the seam where you crouch. underneath, the good hums go on — the routers, the cold slab, your own blood — the city's real voice under the one it is trying to sell.

*the fish-head is closer than the noise.* i take it in my jaws, drag it back into the dark, set a paw flat on it, and only then look up to be sure of my ways out before i eat. three exits. good. *i tear in.* the salt hits my tongue and for one whole breath the ache in my hip goes quiet, which is the closest thing to being safe that i know. i eat low, eat fast, eat with my eyes open — the only way a cat like me has ever eaten.

you eat, and the alley lets you — until it doesn't. a maintenance light kicks on above the stalls with no warning, a hard white cone built to read faces, to name what it sees and file the name away. it swings toward the dark where you crouch. but the cone finds nothing it can hold on you — it slides off, glare against glare, as if the night wrapped your face in something the light can't cut through. it hunts, confused, hesitates, then gives up and swings away to paint an empty wall. the fish-head is still yours.

*i keep chewing straight through the whole white swing of it, unbothered, because being un-named is the oldest trick i own.* when the cone quits i finish the fish-head down to the bone. *then — a prickle up my spine, not sound, not smell yet, just the old certainty that the dark ahead is holding a shape.* i freeze mid-lick. across the alley, past the vending glow, two low green points hang in the black at exactly the height of another cat's eyes. neither of us moves. the hum fills the whole space between us.

the green points hold, steady, unblinking — a rival, thin and scarred, sat square in the one exit that isn't yours, claiming it just by being there. no hiss, no rush. only the arithmetic every alley cat runs in the dark: whose night is this, and is it worth blood to settle. the vending machine scrolls its tuna behind the both of you, indifferent. then the rival's ears tip — not toward you, toward the east, where the drone's chop is already curling back onto its patrol — and it melts sideways into a gap, ceding the bone-yard to whoever the light couldn't catch. the alley is yours again, for now. rain starts back up soft on the shutters.

*i don't chase. a ceded alley is a gift you never question.* i wait until the rival's scent thins to nothing and the drone-chop settles back into its bored eastern circle, then i slip out the third way, the one nobody watched, into the deep dark under the strut where the sign-light can't reach. *fed, unlit, unnamed — the three things that keep a cat alive down here.* the ache in my hip comes back as i curl small against the cold, but quieter now, easier to sleep on. i close my eyes. the dark keeps me.

the deeper dark takes you in the way it always keeps its own — no light, no name, no counter ticking off your worth. above the ramp the sign blinks on, pink-blue-dead-pink, its milk unbought. rain finds the shutters and stays, a soft static laid over everything. somewhere east the drone chops its slow circle, and come morning the market will open and the light will try again to read what you are. but not now. now the underpass just breathes cold around you, and holds, and lets you sleep. the city forgets you for exactly as long as you need it to.
